region: Capital and largest city of Chad
heroText: N'Djamena is Chad's capital, sitting where the Chari and Logone rivers meet opposite Cameroon across the water. First-time visitors should browse the Grand Marché for spices and crafts, see the National Museum of Chad for Sahelian history, and visit the Al-Mouna Cultural Centre for local art and events. N'Djamena International Airport lies just outside the centre, keeping arrivals close to most hotels.

areas.name: Centre-ville
areas.text: Centre-ville around Avenue Charles de Gaulle holds government buildings, banks and the Grand Marché, a practical base close to most main sights.

areas.name: Sabangali
areas.text: Sabangali is a lively riverside district near the Chari River with shops, restaurants and a strong sense of everyday city life.

areas.name: Klemat
areas.text: Klemat is a growing residential district with newer housing, a quieter option for longer stays away from the busiest streets.

areas.name: Moursal
areas.text: Moursal is a bustling central neighbourhood known for markets and nightlife, useful for travellers wanting to be close to daily local activity.

airports.name: N'Djamena International Airport (NDJ)
airports.text: N'Djamena International Airport is less than 3 kilometres from the Grand Marché downtown, making transfers quick once through arrivals formalities.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between N'Djamena International Airport (NDJ) and central NDjamena before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

stayOverview: Base in Centre-ville for walking access to the Grand Marché and government district, or choose Sabangali for riverside local life. Klemat suits quieter, longer stays, while Moursal keeps you close to markets and nightlife.
hotelIntro: N'Djamena hotel choice depends on how central you want to be: Centre-ville and Moursal put markets and daily life within reach, Sabangali adds river views, and Klemat offers a calmer, more residential alternative for longer visits.
rentalCars: A hired driver is more practical than self-drive car rental in N'Djamena, given local traffic conditions and unmarked roads outside the centre.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose Centre-ville for walking access to the Grand Marché and government district, or Sabangali for a livelier riverside stay.

travelTips.title: Getting around
travelTips.text: Arrange a driver through your hotel for getting around, since taxis are informal and fares should be agreed before departure.

travelTips.title: Market visits
travelTips.text: Visit the Grand Marché in the morning for the best selection of spices, textiles and crafts before the midday heat builds.

travelTips.title: Documents and cash
travelTips.text: Carry your passport and keep Central African CFA francs on hand, since card payments are uncommon outside a few larger hotels.

highlights.title: National Museum of Chad
highlights.text: National Museum of Chad is a key NDjamena culture stop, useful for understanding local history, collections and rainy-day planning near the main sightseeing route.

highlights.title: Grand Mosque of N'Djamena
highlights.text: Grand Mosque of N'Djamena anchors the historic and ceremonial side of NDjamena, making it a practical stop for architecture, local memory and orientation.

highlights.title: Avenue Charles de Gaulle
highlights.text: Avenue Charles de Gaulle is a named stop in NDjamena worth keeping on the route when it fits the day's transport, timing and neighborhood plan.

highlights.title: N'Djamena Cathedral

highlights.title: Chari River waterfront
highlights.text: Chari River waterfront adds outdoor time to a NDjamena stay, with open space, views or waterfront breathing room between denser city sights.

highlights.title: Central Market N'Djamena
highlights.text: Central Market N'Djamena gives NDjamena a concrete street-life stop, with food, everyday shopping and local movement that helps visitors read the city.

nearbyIdeas.name: Chari River
nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: The Chari River forms N'Djamena's western edge and the border with Cameroon, with riverside spots good for an easy afternoon outing.

nearbyIdeas.name: Lake Chad
nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: Lake Chad, a longer trip from the capital, is one of the Sahel's key wetlands, though access should be checked in advance for conditions.

history.label: 20th century
history.text: The European district remained a separate part of the city into the 1960s, after independence. Late 20th century Chad gained its independence from France in 1960.

history.label: 1920s
history.text: It was merely a colonial outpost in its early days, and until the 1920s, the city was entirely under French military rule.
On 21 January 1942, a lone German Heinkel He 111 of the Sonderkommando Blaich successfully bombed the airfield at Fort-Lamy, destroying oil supplies and ten aircraft.
Fort-Lamy received its first bank branch in 1950, when the Paris-based Banque de l'Afrique Occidentale opened a branch there.
On 18 November 1956, Fort-Lamy held its first municipal elections.
Before its renaming in 1973, the city was known as Fort-Lamy, named after French army officer Amédée-François Lamy.
The city was partly destroyed during the Chadian Civil War in 1979 and again in 1980.
The city was occupied by Libya during the 1980–81 Libyan intervention as part of the Chadian–Libyan conflict, and the associated Transitional Government of National Unity.
Following differences between Goukouni and Muammar Gaddafi and international disapproval of Libyan intervention, the Libyan troops left the capital and Chad in 1981.
This opened the door to Habré, who marched on N'Djamena, occupying the city with little resistance in 1982 and installing himself as the new president.

history.label: Modern city
history.text: The change to N'Djamena was part of a broader movement to replace colonial names with indigenous ones, reflecting the local Arabic heritage and cultural identity.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: It has since expanded into a major trading city and became the capital of the region and nation.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: During the Second World War, the French relied upon the city's airport to move troops and supplies.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: The tug-of-war reached a conclusion after many months only when Goukouni asked for the intervention of the Libyans, whose tanks overwhelmed Habré's defenses in the capital.
